records.title: Show HN: A decent text-to-image model trained for ~$20K (Apache 2.0 Weights)
records.author: schopra909
records.storyText:
My brother and I run a 2-person lab that trains our own generative video models from scratch. The ultimate goal is a set of creative tools that make it easier for anyone to make animation.

Video models today are too slow/expensive and lack sufficient controls. Creativity is an iterative process. You make, you tweak, you get better. In our opinion, they're not usable yet for storytelling.

When we set out to build Linum v3 (our next video model) earlier this year, the primary goal was to bring the cost envelope of inference down significantly. If our model is fast and cheap, it's the first step (of many) towards useful creative tools.

Typically, you see "latent diffusion models". A VAE (Variational Autoencoder) compresses the input data into a smaller "latent space" and the diffusion model learns how to generate within this subspace.

Over the past few months, we've been publishing our work on efficient pixel-space diffusion models. These throw away the VAE, having the diffusion model learn a latent-space optimized for its exact task.

This serves 3 purposes: 1) Simplify Architecture (no 2-stage model training) 2) Faster Convergence (11x faster convergence vs. our latent diffusion counterpart) 3) Cheaper Inference (4x more aggressive token reduction in attention context-windows, without significant loss in quality)

This past month we were pressure testing our latest architecture (Pyramid-JiT) by training a text-to-image model longer than the typical one-off experiment. Specifically, we trained it for ~$20K on 660M samples.

We were surprised by the quality of results, so we thought we'd release it as open weights for the community (Apache 2.0). The research itself is already public, on our website.

For us, it's a big stepping stone towards cheaper video models, since pretty much all video models start as image models. We like to say these models have to learn nouns before they learn verbs.

records.title: Show HN: Gauge – Open-Source CLI to recursively improve your docs
records.author: 0x63_Problems
records.storyText:
Hi HN, I’m Evan from Gauge. We’re open-sourcing our CLI to recursively improve your docs for coding agents. The CLI includes a local execution backend, so you don't need an account to try it. Explainer video here: https://youtu.be/zhLUlIKB1Mg

The CLI supports a hillclimbing loop:

- set up tasks for coding agents that would need your docs, like 'set up Gauge CI checks'

- run the tasks

- analyze session transcripts for friction or failures

- create variants of your docs to resolve the issues

- re-run the tasks with the doc variants injected (transparently, at the same hostname)

- repeat until you have a variant that resolves the issues

The same loop supports hillclimbing your Skills, CLI, and other agent-facing surfaces.

We started out 2 years ago building open-source developer tools (like Tach https://github.com/tach-org/tach), then pivoted to AI Search optimization, and are now focused on the intersection of the two spaces. We were already working with awesome devtool companies, and they were the first ones to ask us how to optimize for Claude Code and Codex. We realized this would be something that eventually every company needs to do. Our CLI provides primitives for docs/devrel/eng teams to measure, analyze, and improve how coding agents use their product.

The design boils down to two components: VMs and a network gateway.

The VMs are straightforward, we want the agents to be highly privileged within their environment so that they are representative of developers' coding agents. Each VM generally comes with the agent harness itself, language toolchains, and a git repository.

The network gateway is where we terminate TLS and swap in variants of your docs transparently. The gateway also handles credential replacement, so agents see placeholders and can't exfiltrate keys.

The CLI comes with a 'local' execution backend (inference is still remote). For VMs, it uses Docker containers, and the network gateway is mitmproxy running in a sidecar container for each session.

We've used the hillclimbing loop internally to find and fix coding agent issues like mistaken pricing, inaccurate product limitations, and repeated workarounds. We saw coding agents report that Gauge only supports Claude Code and Codex, traced it back to the web pages they fetched, and fixed the behavior (we support Pi, OpenCode, and Antigravity as well). For Clerk, we helped shift coding agents from their legacy 'keyless' mode to their new 'clerk init' command. They were able to validate a pre-release change to their SDK's error messages using Gauge, then saw a 3x increase in coding agents using 'clerk init' post-deploy.

Due to the 'static' nature of AI models, we've realized that closed-loop optimization techniques are now possible for essentially all software products. The same agent can be simulated over and over, meaning that a high-fidelity testing environment is all you need. Achieving the best results boils down to high-quality analysis (finding generalizable friction and objections) and paired experiments (vary only the content, measure the downstream change in behavior).

The repo is here: https://github.com/gauge-sh/gauge-cli and you can start using the CLI with: npm i -g @withgauge/cli

We also have documentation and a quickstart here: https://docs.withgauge.com/agents/guides/cli

If you point a coding agent at those pages, it should guide you through the initial setup - let us know if it doesn't! The intention is for your agent to run some sensible evaluations and find at least one point of friction you can fix.

We'd love to know from HN: Has anyone tried to DIY this locally, or built something in-house at their company? Is this an improvement? If not, what would need to change?

records.title: Show HN: Nico – a two-agent type personal agent on your Mac
records.author: benjushi
records.storyText:
Hi HN. I'm Brian, I make Xmind, the most popular mind mapping app, since 2006. This is my new project Nico, a personal agent for the Mac.

Every huge companies are building personal agents right now. The part I think matters most is the two-agent structure, so that's what Nico is built around.

The front agent talks to you. Always available, only one session, one memory, continuously compaction, and it carries almost no tools, so it can answer fast.

The worker agent does the job. It picks up tasks the front agent puts in an inbox and reports back when they're done. It almost never talks to you; anything it needs goes through the front agent.

I think this is the real step forward, but the attention goes to the cloud computer. I get why: you can hand the agent a task from your phone. But, it also makes everything more complicated. People need to upload the entire environment while

So I built one with the cloud computer taken out. Nico is a native Mac app. You hold the right ⌘ key (or fn) and talk; the front agent answers by voice; the worker agent is pi (github.com/earendil-works/pi) runs by your own AI subscription, in a sandbox.

With computer-use (via cua-driver), browser-use (via a browser extension), and a built-in browser, she can clean up your desktop, or answer "why is my Mac so hot". If you say "this", she looks at the screenshot of the active window. Most tasks run without you; sending an email waits for your click.

The downside: when you're not at your Mac, you can't use it. I haven't figured out what to do about that.

Would you want a personal agent that only lives on your Mac?

records.title: Show HN: Aggregate Finance, your financial data in a spreadsheet you own
records.author: mitchthebaker
records.storyText:
I started building Aggregate Finance a couple of years ago because I was manually updating a Google Sheet to track my credit card statements, monthly recurring transactions, and spending habits. This seemed perfect for automation as I was having to log in to six separate banking apps to pull this information together.

My original intention was to use this tool locally, but I figured it would be an excellent learning opportunity to understand how to scale the application for others to use. The core functionality of Aggregate Finance revolves around syncing banks and brokerages through Plaid to create visuals and data analytics in Google Sheets and OneDrive/Excel, but I've also added Stripe for payments, passkey and TOTP support for MFA (wanted to better learn how WebAuthn works, mostly), and Resend for emailing account updates.

The first question you're likely thinking is: isn't this just reinventing the wheel? There's plenty of other personal finance/budgeting apps out there like Rocket Money, Monarch, Copilot Money, YNAB, Tiller, Credit Karma, etc. I personally tried Rocket Money but it left a bad taste in my mouth how my entire financial history was stored on their servers without having direct ownership of the data. Another pain point with these personal finance apps is you're locked into their subscription and lose access to your financial data if you cancel.

That's why I opted for the Google Sheet and OneDrive/Excel approach since this persists financial data over time and provides direct data ownership. There's a fair argument that these options still share your financial data with Google or Microsoft, so I built a way to download your financial data locally via CSV/Excel/LibreOffice exports.

In terms of data encryption, Aggregate Finance encrypts financial data before it reaches MongoDB: balances, transactions, merchants, statements, holdings, and any user customizations. Each user gets their own AES-256 key rather than a shared key. The reason I went with this approach is for data deletion: when someone deletes their account, their encryption key is deleted as well, so any financial data stored in prior database backups can't be decrypted.

I've been using Aggregate Finance with my own live bank accounts and investment holdings, and it's already been helpful. I can see when my credit card statements are due, monitor my entire investment portfolio, keep track of recurring charges, create budgets, and see how my spending pans out over a given month or over the past year. I'm curious whether it's useful for anyone else, and I'd of course welcome any feedback on how I can improve it. You can try it with a free sample spreadsheet that contains a year of example data with no bank connection required at https://app.aggregatefi.com.

records.title: Show HN: Waymark – A workflow engine that compiles jobs instead of replaying
records.author: icyfox
records.storyText:
Hey everyone! @mozgiii and I have been working on Waymark for the better part of the last year. Waymark’s an open source durable execution library with similar functionality to Temporal or DBOS. A few unique design decisions:

— Write jobs in normal code (right now Python but JS coming soon). Instead of running control flow as-is, which requires booting up an interpreter to replay past state, we’ll just compile your code directly. We walk your AST and map your logic to our stackless VM bytecode. We support variables, conditionals, await, sleep, helper functions, loops... basically what you’d expect in workflow logic.

— Since we’re compiling a language subset, we can proactively flag errors in your workflows locally instead of when they run in production.

— It only requires Postgres as the task broker. We’ve spent a lot of time tuning our design to play nicely with its strengths and limitations; our current benchmarks show around 1500 workflows/second but we still have some more optimization work to do here.

— Actions plug-and-play with FastAPI’s dependency injection syntax. So if you already have an ecosystem based on typehinting/DI, it should fit like a glove.

It allows for parallelization of workflows across one machine or a whole cluster. The bulk of the work per node is done by our central Rust core - which distributes workflows to properly saturate all cores. The idea is to be as batteries included as possible with the broker, webapp, and runtime.

What to use it for? It works great as the runner loop controlling agents, but it also works well for basically any task that you need to kick off in the background. It’s largely replaced our way of writing api code. Most frontend actions at this point just push to a simple REST endpoint that kick off a background job.

I spent an embarrassing amount of time making our https://waymark.sh site interactive - it’s probably the best place to learn more. We’re starting with Python support and looking for community input on what language to ship next. Would love to hear your thoughts!

records.title: Show HN: Cppbolt – A lightweight C++ to WebAssembly compiler written in Rust
records.author: ajtimepyro
records.storyText:
Hey HN! I've been working on cppbolt, a lightweight C++ to WebAssembly compiler written in Rust.

The idea was to build something that can compile and run C++ directly in the browser without downloading a massive LLVM/Clang toolchain.

Unlike projects that bundle LLVM/Clang and can require 100+ MB of compiler assets, cppbolt's compiler payload is around 1 MB. It compiles a supported subset of C++17 directly to standard WebAssembly binaries.

Some things it supports: - Classes, inheritance, virtual functions and operator overloading - Templates and a subset of the C++ standard library - Pointers, references, arrays and dynamic memory - Lambdas, structured bindings and range-based loops

It comes with a browser playground, CLI and npm package.

A few caveats: this is still a work in progress, it doesn't implement the full C++17 standard, and it might not work as expected with certain C++ programs. I'm particularly interested in feedback on the compiler architecture, language support and potential use cases and also interested in connecting with someone who might want to use it in their application.

Try it out: - Playground: https://ajtimepyro.is-a.dev/cppbolt/ - Docs: https://ajtimepyro.is-a.dev/cppbolt/book/ - GitHub: https://github.com/AJTimePyro/cppbolt - npm: https://www.npmjs.com/package/cppbolt

Would love to hear what you think, especially from people who've worked on compilers or WebAssembly.

records.title: Show HN: Firenook – Firebase emulators in Rust: 40× faster writes, 10× less RAM
records.author: sanjevirau
records.storyText:
Hi HN. I build with Firebase almost every day and keep the local emulators running all day, and two things wore me down. The suite is really heavy. Java is required, a heap that grew past 22 GiB on our app, out-of-memory crashes, and data gone at every stop unless you export it. It had become almost unusable and was slowing us down. It's also hard to see what your app is doing. The Emulator UI is incomplete, with no page for Functions, Pub/Sub, Cloud Tasks or Eventarc, only a log.

Firenook replaces the emulators for Firestore, Auth, Storage, Functions, Extensions, and many other services with native Rust services. It's a drop-in replacement, so simply install one npm package, no Java, change `firebase emulators:start` to `firenook emulators:start`, and your firebase.json, ports, SDKs, rules and Functions code stay as they are.

We tested it heavily. On two hours of a real app's traffic, Firenook peaked at 2.11 GiB against 22.57 GiB on official emulator and answered writes in 5.1 ms against 208 ms at the median. On an idle emulator a write is only 1.5× faster and 40× is under load. With --keep-data, millions of documents come back in about 0.5s. Results are here: https://firenook.dev/benchmarks

The console sits on the Emulator UI's port. It shows every function call with its logs and stack, and you can run a failed one again. It shows your rules beside each decision, with the line that decided it, and an inbox of the emails and codes Auth would have sent. Screenshots: https://firenook.dev/console. Honestly, I built the console from scratch as the one the emulators should have had from the start. It's fast, clean, full of the detail you need while developing, and still able to browse and edit millions of documents.

The terminal shows a start-up card, then one line per function call with its outcome and, when it fails, the stack. And `npx firenook mcp add` gives Claude Code, Cursor or VS Code tools over the running emulators, so an agent can read the logs or ask the rules why a request was denied, without touching production.

It's still new and I'm sure it misses things, so if you use the Firebase emulators, I'd love for you to try it on your project. `npx firenook init --adopt --dry-run` checks your project without changing anything. If something behaves differently from the official emulator, please tell me here or open an issue. That's the most useful feedback I can get.

records.title: Show HN: Resource Manager – Manage all resources on the computer
records.author: BIOcanse
records.storyText:
Hello everyone, I'm BIOcanse.

Windows Task Manager has inaccurate readings and limited monitoring items. Various hardware adjustments are also very separated—CPU, GPU, and fans all require their own individual software. Their interfaces and interactions are primitive, and they often overwrite each other's configurations. Moreover, driver management of the CPU and GPU is too clumsy, and the memory usage issue on Windows is also very serious. So I made Resource Manager to view and manage all these resources in one place, making monitoring and scheduling work seamlessly together.

Monitoring:

This software integrates almost every possible monitoring item, letting you look at your computer from a God's-eye view!

Scheduling:

One of the core features. It uses algorithms I wrote to optimize memory usage and reasonably schedule processes across multiple CPU cores. It also supports GPU scheduling, which means it can switch the GPU a program uses while it is running. For example, after launching a game, if GPU usage is high or VRAM is about to overflow, it will move the remaining software to another GPU (for most personal computers, this is usually the integrated GPU).

Reporting:

Many times, computer performance problems are actually just caused by a single program or driver—the benefits of 100 programs optimizing themselves cannot make up for a memory leak in just one program. The reporting page reports abnormal resource usage (CPU, GPU, memory, VRAM, disk read/write, network traffic, and causing system interruptions).

Hardware Adjustment:

All the parameters you can think of for hardware like the CPU and GPU can be adjusted here. However, my own setup is an AMD CPU + NVIDIA GPU, so other setups still need to be verified. I do have several computers with Intel CPUs to verify Intel CPU support, but I really do not have a single AMD GPU. Although most of it uses mature open-source dependencies, there may still be risks, so please use it with caution.

records.title: Show HN: Ferry, a highly customizable and feature-rich file manager for macOS
records.author: jailbirdBD
records.storyText:
I am the main developer of Ferry. The team I am part of began on the demoscene in the mid-90s, but for a long while we are mainly just an indie development studio.

Ferry started with me being forced to use macOS at my current workplace, which suddenly replaced a working environment I'd been using during professional career as a programmer: Windows for around 10 years, then Debian/KDE for the last 15 years.

Over that time, I'd grown very accustomed to Total Commander on Windows, and later Dolphin on Linux as a file manager, plus a collection of small but very useful tools I'd written for myself on Linux. Moving to macOS was quite an adjustment. I really struggled with Finder and the rather fragmented ecosystem of apps, especially when I couldn't find tools that covered the things I was used to having at my fingertips.

Having already written a few internal tools in Swift at work, I started to get familiar with the language while trying out several file managers for macOS without finding one that really suited all of my needs... So one thing led to another, and I eventually decided to build my own version of a better Finder (that's probably how most of the macOS file managers started their journey).

Obviously, the first versions were essentially a combination of a slightly improved dual-pane Finder spiced up with basic features from TC, but t'was more than good enough for me. Once I started sharing it with coworkers and friends they began suggesting features I hadn't even considered initially, many of which turned out to be genuinely useful.

I know there are quite a lot of file managers out there, so a "what makes Ferry different?" is a totally valid question.

Well, Ferry first and foremost tries to be as less opinionated and as much customizable as it's possible, so I have included A LOT of options for personalization. Eg. the layout, the UI, the menus, or the shortcuts are adjustable in many ways, you could even put together something which more or less resembles an old-school Norton Commander-style file manager with a modern toolset if that's your thing.

The app also includes a rather big collection of handy tools and tidbits which probably don't seem too interesting up until the point you run into a specific trivial task, and then you realize you have to search and install a tool for it.

Main features list: https://ferry.indus3.org/#ftrs

Another aspect that's important to me is how the app is made. Having been really involved in the demoscene, I wanted to handcraft as much code as possible and keep AI involvement to a minimum, while still using it to improve quality. Most of Ferry is still written manually, AI mainly helps with the boring parts: proofreading and translations, debugging, tests, temporary tools, code reviews and the site. LLMs have become so advanced that I'm honestly not sure whether this is a good or bad thing for software quality. My skills probably aren't quite on par with a modern LLM agent, but hopefully I can still build something useful and pragmatic by doing most of the work myself.

Licensing follows TC's approach: there's a reminder, but you can keep using the app for as long as you like (or until the reminder gets too annoying). Hopefully that's reasonable enough. But if I eventually become really happy with the codebase, I'll most likely release the source code too.

At this point, since there are plenty of features, I'm becoming much less interested in adding even more of them and rather focused on getting the existing ones as good as possible: size, stability, performance, memory consumption and above all, bugfixes and code quality. Of course I still listen to users, and if someone suggests a feature which is practical and it improves the UX, I try to include it into a future release.

Feel free to contact us, as suggestion and criticism is always welcome!

records.author: ZuraMakaradzeHe
records.storyText:
Hi HN, I'm Zura, and I'm building Revline, a fully agentic video editor.

Revline can take your rough draft of a short or long video, watch it, understand the content, and make edits like a real editor would.

It's been super useful for me (not biased, obviously).

I want to post more content, but my output has never matched how frequently I want to post. Editing takes too much time, and every video I don't finish is waste of time(and money).

The problem I've had (and still have) with current "AI video editors" is that they're either single-purpose, closed, or simply don't work well enough.

If I still have to manually interfere with the timeline when using something advertised as an AI video editor, how much editing is the AI actually doing?

For the same reason, I don't want to use three different platforms for clipping, editing, and creating launch videos. I think those should be features of a single video editor, not separate products.

I like to describe Revline as a general-purpose AI video editor. It isn't limited to rough drafts or turning long videos into short clips. You can also create motion-design launch videos.

I specifically did not included hand-customizations ( like customizing VFX, transition, or even subtitle colors ), because once again, if you have to still hand-edit while using platform to reduce friction of editing, you might aswell save money not using it.

AI can already learn your styles, taste, remember throughout editing, that's the repeatable part every creator/non creator has to do while creating content frequently.

Under the hood

Revline loads agent with 100+ tools to edit video, i have defined set of lanes (Which anthropic calls "Progressive disclosure", but i call it "lanes") to load specific set of skills and tools only needed for specific edit you are working with, so each type of edit gets it's own "harness". Footage is analyzed using Deepgram, Gemini agentic-mode, or handing specific frames to agent directly ( depends on situation ), while motion graphics are generated as React/GSAP components ( hyperframes used as previewing and exporting engine). Rendering runs through FFmpeg and distributed workers. The same editing tools are also exposed over MCP, so Claude Code, Codex, and other agents can edit projects directly.

The entire editor is open-source under Apache 2.0. PRs, contributions, and feedback are welcome!

My ultimate goal is to build a video editing experience that existing platforms simply can't offer.

I'd love to hear what HN thinks, especially where you think an agent-first approach to video editing might fall short.

records.title: Show HN: I paid Claude US$1,070 to read the worst reviews of 30k places to stay
records.author: orifito
records.storyText:
Hi HN, I'm Oriol, a solo developer in Barcelona.

Before booking anything, I used to do the same thing every time: find a place with a great rating, open the lowest-rated reviews and read them one by one. Broken AC, thin walls, a bed as hard as a board, a shower that barely works. Very often the deal-breaker was right there, written by guest after guest, under a lovely 8.9 global score.

OKstays does that reading for you. It scores 33,000+ places to stay in 95 destinations on how well you'll actually sleep and stay there, and ranks them for how you travel (light sleeper, remote work, family...).

This month I re-scored 30,500 places from what guests wrote. For each one, Claude reads its newest and lowest-rated reviews, then a second search collects what about 7 other review and booking sites say. It scores 67 comfort signals from 0 to 10, each with a short reason you can read on the place's page. If a deal-breaker (dirty rooms, an uncomfortable bed, a poor shower, bugs) ends up at 6.0 or below, the place is left out of every ranking. One angry guest can't do that alone: it has to be a pattern.

What came out (method and charts: https://okstays.com/stats/deal-breakers): - 1 in 39 places to stay has a deal-breaker guests keep reporting. - Half of them come down to a poor shower (51%). Bugs are next (35%). - 92% of them still have a guest rating of 8+. Across all places, it's 97%. - Under US$100 a night, deal-breakers are nearly 4.5x as common as at US$400+. - Among hotels: about 1 in 5 in New Delhi, 1 in 19 in Mexico City, and 1 of 698 in Tokyo.

The cost, because HN always asks: about US$1,070 in API calls, US$3.7 cents a place, all batched (first search ~US$1.3c, second search ~US$1.2c, scoring ~US$1.2c). Before spending it, I tested methods against places I had researched in depth. My old scores were off by about 1.1 points on average; reading reviews brought that to about 0.5 (on a different, larger reference set, so read it as a direction, not a precise gain).

It's free, no sign-up, and it also works inside ChatGPT, Claude and Grok as a connector (okstays.com/mcp). It earns booking commissions, and hotels can't pay to rank or to be removed. Last month it earned its first US$8.81, 18 months after I started. That was also the first money I ever made online.

Two things I'd love from you: pick a city you know well and tell me if the top 5 feels right. Thank you!

records.title: Show HN: teletap – Your remote coding agents ask you when stuck
records.author: megalomanu
records.storyText:
Hi HN!

I'm Manuel, CTO of Tandem.

Most of our PRs are now written by custom coding agents on remote hosts. But we had a recurring problem: they sometimes lacked product context and consequently guessed too much. This resulted in some PRs coming back a bit off, with some wrong choices. We ended up spending more time fixing the PRs than if we had made them ourselves.

So we built teletap, first for ourselves, and now for everyone. How it works: when an agent is stuck on something it can't find itself, it asks a person on the team. It picks the best person to help it, based on a short "when to ask" description each developer specifies, like "pricing owner", or AGENTS.md instructions. The question pops up on that engineer's computer. They answer it, and it goes straight back into the agent's session, which is now unblocked and can continue. If the engineer doesn't know, they just have to say so, and the agent will ask someone else.

Many teams use Slack for this. We tried it too. But we didn't find it productive enough. The agent had to keep checking a thread. An idle session never saw the reply. With teletap, the answer is delivered directly into the session, even if it's idle.

It works with Claude Code, Codex, Gemini, Hermes and Pi. Just install it on a device (your computer, a VM, a Docker container, a VPS...), and it finds all the installed agents and plugs into them. We were inspired by Tailscale, which we love. Devices talk peer-to-peer, encrypted end to end, and fall back to our relay only when a direct path is impossible (the relay never sees the content). It's very minimal: you don't have to live in another interface.

In case you're wondering, we wrote it in Rust and everything runs over QUIC, on a single UDP socket. The most fun part of the project was the integration with agents, figuring out how to put the answer into a live session. For instance, Claude Code has an internal messaging socket (CLAUDE_CODE_MESSAGING_SOCKET), while the messaging for Codex works through its app-server. For pi, we developed a plugin (how surprising).

Short video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=z224uyyxuYQ

Website with install instructions: https://teletap.dev

We'd love your feedback, especially from teams that run agents in the cloud.
